utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber through me wishes to bid good morning to all those present. I know that for at least two of you, this is your second case, that some started at 8.00 in the morning despite the snow. Today we have a hearing devoted to a witness, but before we do that, there are several points to deal with. First of all, I should like to refer to the fact that in the motion regarding judicial notice of certain facts, the Defence has conveyed its opinions regarding the response of the Prosecution a few days ago. If the Prosecution wishes to respond to the submissions of the Defence, you may do so up until the end of this week but not later. So, Mr. Mundis, if you wish to do that, you are authorised to respond. Yes, I give you the floor.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have nothing to add at this point in time. We -- if we choose to make a further filing, we will do so by the end of this week. Thank you.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Several days ago, I raised the question of a book which a witness sent to the Registry. This book was not translated, and I would like to ask both parties what their position is. Do they wish the book to be translated and that the full translation be tendered into evidence, or the other possibility would be to simply return the document to its owner through the Registry. So I have asked you to take a position about this, but to this day we have not received any submissions. We would like to know what your positions are. Mr. Mundis.

I don't believe we have them with us in the courtroom now. With respect to the remaining portions of that book, it's unclear to us whether that's the same material that the Office of the Prosecutor has in its possession or additional material, and as of this point in time, we have not made any arrangements with the Registrar to review that material to see if in fact it's the same or if, in fact, it's a different volume of the book that the -- that we have in our possession. But again, our view with respect to the previously indicated pages of that book that the Chamber wanted translated, we do have that available and we can make that available to the Trial Chamber later this morning if the Trial Chamber still wishes to have those portions which the Trial Chamber directed us to translate.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Abid Izmirlic. I was born on the 13th of April, 1961, in the village of Klotjevac, municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have an occupation or position today? If so, which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am employed in the federal defence ministry. I am an official in charge of the certain segments of the cadaster of property of the Federation and land regulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question that I put to all witnesses, in 1992 and 1993, which is more than ten years ago, what was your position? What were you doing in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, I was a fighter in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was in the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have a rank and, if so, what was it and what unit were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a rank in the former JNA, which I left in 1992, with the rank of captain. And in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I received a rank in 1997, and that was the rank of major. In 2001, I opted for a non-military status, and I still enjoy that status today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You haven't quite answered my question. I'm asking about 1992 and 1993. Which unit were you assigned to, which headquarters, which entity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, in April -- or, rather, May, I was commander of the battalion of the Otes detachment until September, and then I was redeployed to the defence ministry at the time, and I stayed there until January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And after January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was officially assigned to go to Zagreb to obtain geotopographic material for the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Because of the well-known conflicts that occurred in the territory of Bosnia with the members of the HVO, I was unable to return to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Have you testified before in and international or national court about the events that took place in your country or is this the first time for you to testify as a witness in a court of law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have not testified before. This is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Defence who begin with the examination-in-chief, which will be relatively brief as we are due to have the break in about 20 minutes, I should like to give you some explanations regarding the way in which this hearing will evolve so that we can ensure the smooth functioning of the proceedings. As I had said a moment ago, you have been called by the Defence to contribute to some technical clarifications about certain facts that took place. You will therefore be asked to answer questions that will be put to you by the Defence. These questions will be quite neutral, and you will be asked to provide quite detailed answers to those questions. Upon the completion of this question and answer period, the Prosecution, situated to your right, will also be asking you questions within what is known as the cross-examination, and the duration of those questions will be roughly as long as the time spent by the Defence. You will note, however, that the form of the questions put to you during the cross-examination will be different, because the party cross-examining may ask leading questions, and the witness may answer with a yes or no. Upon the completion of this stage, the Defence attorneys may have some additional questions for you linked to the questions put during the cross-examination. The three Judges in front of you, if they feel fit, may ask you questions. As a rule, they have two aims, either to clarify the answers you have given or because they believe that you are in a position to make some useful contribution in the interest of justice, and they will have questions for you along those lines. During the questioning, the parties may show you documents, and if they do so, you will be asked to recognise the document and perhaps comment on those documents. I also have to draw your attention to two points. You have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, which means that false testimony is excluded, and I'm sure you understand that. And the second point, which is quite specific to our procedure, and that is that a witness may refuse to answer a question if he feels that the answer may one day be used against him to incriminate him. In that case, which is something we never encountered so far, the witness may say that he doesn't wish to answer, but the Chamber may request that he answer it nevertheless, guaranteeing him immunity from prosecution. So those would be in broad lines the instructions for the proceedings. In about 20 minutes we will have a break, and we will have another one in about an hour and a half. Your testimony may be completed today. If not, we will continue tomorrow. I also draw your attention to the fact that this is an oral procedure, so we have no written documents about what you're going to say, hence the importance of your answers, because they will constitute part of the transcript. You will see the screen in front of you with the text in English, and this becomes a part of the file. Should you have any difficulty, please do not hesitate to tell us. We have another 15 minutes or so until the break. I shall give the floor to the Defence to begin their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, at the beginning I should like to provide certain documents which I intend to use during the examination-in-chief of this witness. We have copies for all the participants in the proceedings, and one copy has prints in colour which should be given to the witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning, Mr. Izmirlic.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We have had the opportunity to meet before your testimony today before the Trial Chamber, but for the purpose of the transcript, allow me to introduce myself. My name is Stephane Bourgon, and I am accompanied today by my colleague Ms. Edina Residovic and as well as by a legal assistant Muriel Cauvin, and together we represent the accused General Hadzihasanovic. Mr. Izmirlic, I would like to immediately ask you it take the documents that are before you and to turn to tab number 1. Tab number 1, Mr. Izmirlic, can you confirm that we have discussed this document together in the presence of an interpreter yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I only ask this question, Mr. Izmirlic, simply to go quicker into the procedure so that we can get immediately into the substance. I would simply like to go to page 2. I will read the information on your professional experience, which is at this page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, just a small technical matter. The document under tab 1, it has -- bears the confidential stamp. If you're referring to it now, does that mean that you're moving its confidentiality?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that we can lift the confidentiality of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We take note of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] [In English] ... what was included in this document with respect to your professional experience and ask you to confirm whether this corresponds to your knowledge and experience. From 1980 to 1984, Mr. Abid Izmirlic attended the Belgrade Military Academy. He graduated in 1984 and obtained a diploma in geodesy with a speciality in topography. From 1988 to 1992, he was an instructor on military topography in Sarajevo. He left the JNA in April 1992 and began working for the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the beginning of 1993, he was sent to Croatia to work with the Croatian Ministry of Defence in the topography division. In March 1994, he reported to the Supreme Command Staff in Sarajevo to assist the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he was sent to work for the chief of staff of the ARBiH in Kakanj, General Hadzihasanovic, who gave him the assignment to build the relief of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a model, part of which was used in the present case. In 1997, he was promoted to the rank of major and worked in the Ministry of Defence in the geodesy topographic support department. In 2001 he authored a book on topography for the use of the army of the Federation. In 2002, he retired from the army. Mr. Izmirlic, I would simply ask whether this corresponds to your professional background.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Almost entirely, yes, with the addition that in 1992, as I said, up until September, I was a professional soldier and battalion commander in the Otes detachment until I transferred to the defence ministry. And finally under point 13, I chose my future status to be a civilian official in the defence ministry. According to what you said, it emerged that I was a retiree, but I continue to be employed in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I just have one more question concerning the information provided in this section and with regards to your assignment to Croatia in 1993. Is there a reason why you were sent to work with Croatia in the topography department? Is there something you were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. supposed to get there?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the aggression began against Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, all the originals of topographic maps which were used up until then within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina were taken away to Belgrade so that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was left without prints of topographic maps and also without the originals from which copies could be printed for the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I needed to get either prints or originals of topographic maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Izmirlic. We move on to the subject matter of your testimony today, and my first question is whether the methodology which is described in this document at tab 1 and which we discussed yesterday, does that correspond to what you were asked to do and what you did to accomplish this task?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no objection to leading questions with respect to the background of this witness, but we do object to a procedure whereby my learned colleague reads from a Defence pleading and asks the witness to comment on that. We certainly believe it's important for the witness to describe his -- the instructions he received and the methodology that he undertook in complying with the instructions he received from the Defence, but we believe this is information that should be asked in a non-leading way so that the witness can fully describe to the Trial Chamber exactly what he was asked to do and exactly how he did that without the benefit of a -- of simply confirming what's in a written pleading that was prepared and filed by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon. The Prosecution would like the witness to answer these technical matters rather than you stating things and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. My learned colleague is quite right. I just wanted to save some time by going to the first question, but I would like the witness to explain everything that he did. I was just trying to move more quickly, but my learned friend is quite right, and I have no problems with his objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Izmirlic, I would like you to turn to tab number 2. My question concerning tab number 2 is whether this chart contains the 15 scenarios you were asked to assess and provide conclusions on?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will now proceed, Mr. Izmirlic, to ask you a few technical questions before looking at exactly the work that your performed. And my first question to you would be as follows: What are the factors which affect the possibility for an individual to distinguish or to see a person, an object, or an event from various distances?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: On condition that there is optical visible between two points, any two points on the ground along the line of observation, the clearness of the picture obtained depends on a number of factors, and those are the time of day, the season, the weather, the position and size of the object being observed, the distance between the person observing the object and the object, also the contrasting colours surrounding the object and the visual capacity of the observer. Those are the main factors on which the clearness of the picture depends. It depends -- I can elaborate on even of these factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 10.30. We need to have our technical break. I am told that we need to have a break of at least 30 minutes because there are some technical matters to address. So we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume. I hope that the technical problems have been resolved, and I hope that Mr. Bourgon's computer is working properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My colleagues will try to resolve the difficulty, but we'll continue, because I won't need this equipment until the last part of my examination-in-chief. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] We've lost some time, so we'll try to make up for that time by maybe trying to keep the answers as short as possible, and if I need more, then I can ask you for more. Before the break, you gave -- in response to my question, you gave a series of factors which influenced the possibility for someone to see or distinguish a person. Is there a difference when you see -- when you say to distinguish an object and to see an object? Is there a difference between these terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I'm not sure -- I'm not sure this witness -- there's any foundation for this witness to be able to answer any of these types of questions other than simply a general knowledge that anyone in this courtroom might be able to have, and to that extent I'm not sure that his testimony will bring much to us. If my learned colleague can lay some kind of a foundation as to the ability of this witness to answer these types of questions, I'm not sure that this takes us much farther than the common knowledge that all of us have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, Mr. Mundis, as far as this objection is concerned, Defence counsel would like to know whether the witness as a technical expert can distinguish between the distinguish and see. Perhaps he could answer the question, perhaps not. And then we'll see what the situation is. Now, please answer the question that Defence counsel put to you. Do you make a distinction between those terms or not? If not, it's not necessary to waste time on an issue, on a question that can be dealt with very rapidly. Please answer the question. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There is a distinction between seeing an object or people. To see an object or people means to have a clear view of the object observed. For example, if it's a man, part of the body, the colour of the person's hair, et cetera. To distinguish something means that the observer doesn't have such a clear view. It only means that you can distinguish an object at a certain distance. You can tell whether it's a tree or a man, but as to what the man is wearing, as to the colour of his clothes, et cetera, these are things that one cannot see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Izmirlic. My next question is simply: Is there a method or a way to determine if a person was able to see an object, a person, or an event from where he was located?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are very clear scientific methods. It's not necessary to be in a particular field. I wasn't in this area, the area concerned, but there are methods. There's a graphic method for depicting the lie of the land. Then there's the graphic method that is used by uses triangles. And there's a computer method to calculate angles. It's quite possible to determine scientifically whether a certain object is visible or not from a certain distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in response to my first question, you mentioned something as to whether there was optical visibility as being the primary factor before you went into the other factors. Can you explain how you go about assessing this optical visibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Again, Mr. President, our position is this -- there's no foundation for a topographer fear to be testifying about optical visibility or optics. If my learned colleague can lay such a foundation and show that the witness has some kind of technical expertise with respect optics we have no problem with this. But the witness is a topographer. He is not an optician, he is not an expert in optics. At least based on the material before us which consists of a pleading or a filing that my learned colleagues have put before this Court. We don't have any kind of foundation for any kind of testimony on it technical aspect of what the witness is being asked to testify about. Topography is one thing. Optical visibility, capacity of eyesight, there's no foundation whatsoever for this type of testimony coming in via this witness unless my learned colleagues can lay some kind of a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, there is an objection. Could you ask the witness whether as a topographer or given his military experience he had any training in optics. Try to know what he knows about the field of optics, because the Prosecution claims that he has no knowledge about optics. But if you have called him here it's probably because you believe he has such knowledge. Please ask him the appropriate questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the transcript I would like to state we have filed a document which quite clearly explains what Mr. Izmirlic was asked about. It mentioned the questions to be put to him during the examination-in-chief, and as far as the issue of optical visibility is concerned, this has nothing to do with the eyes. It's a topographic method that a topographer use. So this should not be a problem. It shouldn't be problematic, and I would like to ask the question. I'd like to put the witness -- I'd like to put the questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have heard the Prosecution's objection to your ability as a topographer to answer a question that concerns optical visibility, but it appears that you're quite capable of answering this question. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our eye forms an image, and one can say metaphorically that it's an optical instrument. In all material that I have had and in all schools that I attended and given all the methods I have used, this is the term used, optical visibility. One tries to assess whether there was optical visibility or not. What our eye can see is what we call optical visibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And is there a method, Mr. Izmirlic, that you can use based opened your technical abilities to determine whether it was possible to see, for a person to even see an object from a distance?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you explain briefly what this method is?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: If you use a method to determine the lie of the ground, it's necessary to have a topographic map. In this case, I was provided with topographic maps of the territory where the observed points were located. By marking the observation points and the point observed -- we marked the observation points and the points observed, and then you determine the height at the -- in the direction concerned. A graphic method is used to determine the configuration of the land. By linking up these points, as the crow flies, you have the distance as the crow flies or, rather, this is the direction that the human eye looks in. This is what we call optical visibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Izmirlic. I would like you to come back to the issue of those 15 scenarios that you were asked to assess and I would like you to say whether on the basis of this method there were any of these scenarios it was not possible to see an object in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether I can use the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You can use table 3 or if you could go at tab number 3 in the documents that were provided to you.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Here I have a table of basic information on the directions observed. There are 15 directions that I analysed. I used the already-mentioned methods, and I compiled this table. In the first column you have the number of the direction in question. In the second column of the direction observed, the name of the observation observed. For example, under number one we have Strmac. Later in the documents you will see that this direction has been marked with an A. B was used to mark Gornje Cukle. Gornje Cukle. That was the point that was observed. The third column refers to the air distance in metres between those two points. The next column is the altitude of the observation point marked with H -- marked by HA. That is the altitude above sea level. The next column is the altitude of the point observed marked with HB. And then in the next column you have the difference in altitude between those two points. If there's a minus in front of the difference in altitude, this means that the observer was at a higher altitude in relation to the point observed. And then the following column is the altitude of the obstacle on the territory if there was such an obstacle. And then finally in the last column there are conclusions drawn as to whether it was possible to observe in this direction or not, whether observation was possible in this direction or not. In the footnote, it says that air distances were measured and altitude read from topographic maps the scale of which was 1:25000. And these maps were adopted as a set of maps, number 5. The second note states that the evaluation of the observation of points was done by the method of ground profiles and by using the method of triangles. That's also graphic method. And then there was also calculation that was carried out of position angles in these directions. I can support all of this with the literature. In the footnote it says that detailed instructions for these methods or, rather, operations can be found in the textbook Military Topography written by Abid Izmirlic dated 2001. And then the book entitled Military Topography by Gvozden Colovic, 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Izmirlic. I look at your conclusions in the last column of this chart, and I see that for the scenarios 1, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15, it says that observation was not possible. Was this a conclusion based on the method that you've just described, and what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Given the methods I have mentioned for calculating the ground profile in these directions, that was the case. And then there was the method of triangles and the method of calculating position angles, and the conclusions are identical for the directions that you have just mentioned. There was no optical visibility. And this means that the configuration of land was such that there were obstacles so that a potential observer can't or could not see with his naked eye or an instrument of any kind the points in these directions. There was no observation possible in these directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question is I would like to refer you to tab number 4, and I would like you, using the ELMO which is beside you, to run through these documents and explain exactly the work that was performed by yourself. And if you have some charts or maps, to put them on the ELMO and everyone will be able to follow in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: This is the first direction, marked number 1, Strmac-Gornje Cukle. The next attachment is a segment on excerpt from a topographic map, the scale of which is 1:25000. Point A is marked on the map as I have already said. That is the point of observation. And B marked the point observed from the observation point. The next attachment is also an excerpt from that same topographic map, and we have the direction A and B. In the lower part we in fact have the configuration of the land, which was obtained in the following way: The horizontal line refers to the topographic distance between these two points, and the scale is 1:25000 as can be seen. This means that 1 millimetre represents 25 metres in real life. On the vertical line we have the altitude of the points on entire direction. The scale is 1:10000 to make it easier to have a clear picture. The entire direction also refers to the altitude. The altitude of all points is marked on the entire direction, the altitude that intersects our direction. This is a complete profile, because the altitude of each isohypses is read. An isohypses is a closed curved line which connects points at an identical altitude. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. By vertically descending to altitude points and linking up these points and forming an uninterrupted line, you obtain the exact configuration of the land, the profile of the land, such as -- such as it is on that direction. And again, when you link up this red line, when you link up points A and B to form a line, you obtain the direction of observation. If there's an obstacle in this direction, this red line, so to speak, cuts through the hill. In this case, it means that we have no optical visibility between those two points. I would also like to point out that the distance between those two points is 4.200 metres. The next attachment is an enlarged version of this very same segment. On the Y axis we have the scale 1:20000, and the X axis or the vertical line the scale is 1:8000. That is the method used to calculate the configuration or profile of the land, and this shows the entire configuration of the land in that direction. To confirm what I have just said, I used the method of triangles or, rather, I assessed visibility by using the method of triangles. I provided the altitude of point A, point B, and the altitude of the obstacle on that direction, and then I provided the distance between those two points, the two points of the direction and the distance to the obstacle if there was an obstacle hindering visibility. The triangle method is used as follows: On the horizontal, rather, Y line, you take the lowest altitude as a 0 value. In this case, this is -- this altitude is 610 metres. This was taken to be value 0. Point A or, rather, the point from which one observed, was 330 metres above this altitude point, and the scale is 1:10000. And there is a vertical line, 33-millimetre vertical line heading towards another point. In this case, there is an obstacle which is higher than the observation -- the point observed. It was 38 metres higher than the point observed. When you link up these two extremities, these two points, A and B, and B and P are linked up, you can see that the triangle at point P is above the observation point. This means that you have no optical visibility in this direction. Again by using -- by calculating the position angles of this big triangle and of the small triangle, the position angle is an angle that includes the horizontal direction and the direction towards a certain object. In this case, capital S is the local angle -- the position angle of this big triangle or, rather, it's the main direction of observation. And small s is the position angle in relation to the obstacle. In this case, small s is bigger than capital S, and this means that in this direction there is no optical visibility. From everything that has been said, by using these three methods I can claim with full responsibility that in the direction in question, Strmac-Gornje Cukle, there was no visibility, and it wasn't possible to observe with the naked eye or an instrument of any kind the point in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to refer you to this first page of this -- those documents which is the map which indicates points A and B, and I would ask that you place this on the ELMO, please. And my question is: In marking points A and B on this map, did you use grid references, and how exactly did you determine the position of the observer, the letter A, and the position of the object being observed, the letter B?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: In all segments or, rather, directions, I chose the most favourable points for the observer, the points that are dominant, that are higher in altitude than all the other points. So the most favourable position for the observer. Similarly, the most favourable position for point B, as can be seen from all the attachments of topographical maps where the most dominant features or points were selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now refer you to tab number 11 in those documents, and I would ask that you perform the same exercise with respect to scenario number 8, but of course without going into as much -- as many details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, for the benefit of the Judges, we have followed very well the reasoning of the witness. On map 1, could he show us with the pointer where is the obstacle at grid 640 metres, at an altitude of 640 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Point A is the position of the observer, point B that which is being observed. At a distance of 3.750 metres from the observer, there is an obstacle at an altitude of 648 metres, and the target or the point of observation is at an altitude of 610 metres. At this position at this place, there is the obstacle which prevents visibility of the point of observation. Science tells us that to the obstacle in this case one should add 10 metres to deal with certain natural obstacles such as a tree, which I did not do in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So will you point the pointer at the point 648 metres so that we can clearly see where the obstacle is, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] We now move to tab 11 and scenario 8.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: The next direction is Grahovcici-Gornje-Cukle. Again we have an insert from a topographical map in the scale of 1:25000 with points A and B marked on the map. An excerpt from the topographical map of the direction A and B with a profile of the ground calculated in the same way as I explained for the previous scenario. By linking points A and B, one can see that this imagined line of visibility cuts across the relief in several places, which means that along this direction or axis again there is no optical visibility, and it is not possible to observe anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, out of curiosity, can you explain to the Trial Chamber why would a soldier be interested in doing this type of exercise?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: I am not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What is the utility of doing this exercise for a soldier or a commander?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Such assessments must not happen. In his office, he must first prepare all possible directions of observation, because along this direction you can't even establish radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to your -- if you can finalise this assessment with scenario number 8, and if you move to the triangle method that you use.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Along this direction or axis, that is the distance between these two points is 3.075 metres. The altitude of point A, the point of observation, is 680 metres. Point B, which is being observed, is at an altitude of 600 metres. And the highest obstacle along this direction is 708 metres high, which by drawing these triangles shows clearly that there is no obstacle visibility along this direction. The method of angles shows that small s is larger than capital S, which again confirms that along this direction there's no optical visibility and it is not possible to carry out any kind of observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on to tab number 12. Can you quickly go through scenario number 9.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the direction Grahovcici, hamlet of Milika, and Gornje Cukle. On this attachment we also have points A and B marked. The next attachment is an insert of the topographical map of this direction and an image of the ground profile and relief of the ground providing the same method, and by linking the two extreme points it is clear that the red line intersects the hill in many places. So again there's no optical visibility along this direction. This is an enlargement of the same insert in the stale indicated, 1:16756 and 1:6000 along the vertical axis. Again using the method of triangles, I measured another hill with another triangle because there are three large obstacles along this direction. I calculated three -- two triangles, I'm sorry. Point A has an altitude of 725 metres, point B 605 metres, one obstacle has an altitude of 705 metres, and the other one 663 metres. Applying the triangle method by indicating the differences in altitudes, it is visible that there's no optical visibility as confirmed by calculating the angles as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on to tab number 13 and scenario number 10. If you can just give your conclusions using only the first profile map.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a problem on the transcript. It's working now. Please ask him the question again appearing in line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Provide your conclusion with respect to scenario number 10. So I have to repeat the question, but again just quickly go through the maps and give your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the direction Grahovcici or rather the hamlet of Plavcici to Gornje Cukle, an excerpt from the topographic map, and it is clear that there are one, two, three hills along this line. Our red line cuts across those hills, which means that along this direction no optical visibility can be achieved. Also using the triangle method and the method of calculating the triangles. And I claim with full responsibility that along this direction, too, there is no optical visibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would now ask you to do the same exercise but again very quickly with tab 14, scenario 11.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: This is the line from Dusina to Lasva. That is the surroundings of the school in Lasva. On the map segment with the points A and B indicated. Then we have the method of calculating the profiles and though the distance between those two points is 1.750 metres, there is a large hill. So any potential observer could not achieve optical visibility because of it. This is an enlargement of the segment. And the graphic method of triangles is as follows. Only if point B were to be within this large triangle would there be optical visibility. This is also confirmed by calculating the triangles, applying the triangle method.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now draw your attention to tab 15, and without putting it on the ELMO, simply turn to the page that has the first profile analysis and provide your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Here again the direction is from Dusina, that is the cemetery, to the crossroads in Lasva. The distance is 1.775 metres, and there are two hills which are preventing any kind of visibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the same thing for tab 16, which corresponds to scenario 13.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: The direction Nova Bila to Guca Gora, along this direction, and the distance is 5.850 metres, and there is no optical visibility as can be seen on this profile of the ground because the hill is obstructing the view. And at this distance, it is not possible to achieve any kind of visibility, and I think this is a case that is quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you do the same thing for tab 17 and scenario 14.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: It's the direction between Cifluk and Donje Maline. Again by using the method of profiles, we see that there are two hills standing in the way at a distance of 2.700 metres, 3.050 metres. So it is not possible to achieve optical visibility. And this could be confirmed by applying the triangle methods and the position angle method.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as for tab 18, which corresponds to scenario 15.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: The configuration of the land along the direction Velika Bukovica-Guca Gora is such that almost immediately in front of the observer there is an obstacle, a hill, so that along this direction it is simply not possible to achieve optical visibility, because almost along the whole length of this direction we have the red line cutting across the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Izmirlic. My next question would be as follows: For all of these scenarios that we've just covered, if a person were to say that they were able to see an object at point B when they were located at point A, what would be your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: My conclusion is absolutely that in all these cases, nine different directions, it is not possible to achieve any visibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now refer you back to tab number 3, considering that this leaves us with six scenarios, and can you tell the Trial Chamber what your conclusion was for these six scenarios, and I refer to scenarios number 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Along these directions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, stop. The Prosecution is on its feet. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I also observe from tab 3 there are two additional scenarios, that is 14 and 16, which the English version at least indicates that observation was also possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must say that it is an error made at night. The two additional scenarios which are present here are repetitions. So I must draw the attention of the Chamber to an error in this table which needs to be corrected. We put the wrong page in the binder. So scenario 14 is a repetition of 7, and so is scenario number 16. Consequently, Mr. President, scenario number 14 on this table can be scratched. Scenario number 15 becomes 14, and scenario 16 can also be redacted. And scenario number 17 becomes 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Mundis, have you taken note of this? Very well. Please continue, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Izmirlic, for the scenarios from 2 to 7 in which you mention that -- where it says that an observation was possible, is there a way for a layman to determine whether it was possible to see or to distinguish a person, an object, or an event in the circumstances described in these scenarios?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. These same directions that you have listed were also analysed and ground profiles were done for them, and it is obvious from the image of the ground profile or the relief of the ground there is optical visibility. Once that is established, we tried to establish what it is possible to see at such a distance counting on all the factors which may facilitate or complicate visibility, but along these directions there is optical visibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what type of information would you use in order to determine what you can see from those distances?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: I used the standards or tables from literature available to me, or, rather, the quoted book by Professor Gvozden Colovic from 1979 where there are standards for certain scenarios as to what can be seen from certain distances, and we can provide this as an attachment. Also, norms taken from the rules, soldier, detachment infantry 1970 used by the former JNA. Since that was not sufficient for me either, I verified those tables on the ground, and true enough I did not visit these actual spots that are mentioned because there was a lot of snow in Sarajevo and I didn't think it necessary for me to go there, but in the surroundings of Sarajevo, I carried out a test, and I asked myself some even broader questions which I could read out to you or, rather, the questions that I wanted to find the answers to so that I could be 100 per cent sure of what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I draw your attention to tab 19, and if you can explain what this information is.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: This is a table of possible observations on the ground. The data were taken from the book military topography by Gvozden Colovic as I indicated, and there's an indication of the objects that are being Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. observed as examples and the distances. Again there's a technical error as can be checked with the original version of the book. This is not with binoculars the distances at which objects can still be distinguished. That is the original expression from the book, the book military topography by Gvozden Colovic. So in this table a printing error has been made it says with binoculars in the B/C/S version. But, rather, with the naked eye. And then you see certain norms that show that at a distance of 5 kilometres that it is possible to distinguish a house, or that a lonely tree can be seen at a distance of 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would just like if you can turn to page 65 of the attachment in this tab 19 and say whether this is the correct version of the book that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the book translated into English, but in my own language it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's go further down. In your own language, page 65 of the attachment in your own language.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry. I will try to be more clear. You have those two pages. Then there's an attachment that follows in tab 19. Do you have that? There's a number, 5158, Vojna Topografija?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In this attachment, did you say what this attachment is?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: This is a copy of the book Military Topography which we quote from, its table of consents and the table that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you move to tab 20 and say what this is?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: This is a table of possible observation from the "Rules, Soldier, Infantry Detachment" from the year 1980. And we have certain norms here. For example, a soldier who is moving can be seen from a distance of 850 metres. For example, one can see the head of a man at -- from a distance of 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where does this information come from?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: As I have said, this information was taken from the book Military Topography by Gvozden Colovic and from the rules soldier infantry detachment, and these were rules used by the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the pages that follow this table, is that the book you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For the record, I note that this is Defence Exhibit number 1642. I now move on to tab 21, and I would like you to put this map on the ELMO and explain exactly what this is.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: As I have said, I was not able to see the actual directions where there was optical visibility. I wasn't able to go into the field. And since I didn't find all the answers to some of the questions I was interested in, I made a test in the vicinity of Sarajevo, in the surroundings of Sarajevo, and I asked myself a number of questions, and I suggest that I read them out rapidly. For example, if there's optical visibility in a given direction, what can be seen from a certain distance? The questions are as follows: Is it possible to see a man? Can one distinguish the sex and age of people, whether someone is a boy or a girl? Is it possible to distinguish between a soldier and a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just to indicate to everyone that that is actually the information included in tab 24. Sorry, in tab 24, yes.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, is it possible to distinguish hodja, priest, or a nun in a group of people. Or soldiers? Is it possible to identify a uniform, whether military or police. Is it possible to see the insignia of the army or police? Is it possible to differentiate the types of weapons? Is it possible to see rank markings? Is it possible to see what is being carried, a mortar or a machine-gun or, for example, a television or a fridge? Is it possible to distinguish a type of vehicle used, a passenger car, a tractor, a truck, or a bus? Is it possible to clearly see the mark of a vehicle, for example, Golf, an Opel, a Ford or a Renault? And is it possible to see licence plates, the licence plate number. Is it possible to identify a driver, whether the driver is a soldier, a male or female? Question 14, is it possible to see what is loaded on the truck, cattle or objects, for example, a sofa, a fridge, a cupboard, a TV, a video, or weapons. And then 15, is it possible to distinguish the following objects: Houses, stables, garages? My next question: Is it possible to see items inside a building through an open window? My following question: Is it possible to distinguish the people in the vicinity of a building? And then the last question I put to myself was whether it was possible to see fire and smoke coming from the building on fire. Using the norms and the literature that was available, I, as I have said, put these 18 questions to myself, and I wanted to provide an answer to these questions. I wanted to be able to state what one could see from certain distances, certain directions where there was optical visibility. I referred to distances of 850 metres, 1.400 metres, 2.550 metres, 2.700 metres, 2.825 metres, and 3.050 metres. These are the six distances I referred to or, rather, the six areas in which we determined that there was optical visibility. I carried out this test in the surroundings of Sarajevo -- or, rather, to be more precise, in a place called Bojnik. I climbed onto a house that was being built, a house that was at a higher altitude than everything else in that area, and I could clearly see the direction I was observing from that point. Earlier on, using a topographic map, I identified certain points on this road, and I marked those points. I had previously gone there with my friend and identified these points, and as you can see, here we have the observation point from which I observed with my naked eye and by using a pair of binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I notice, Mr. Izmirlic, I look at this map which is on the ELMO, and I look at location number 5. It says here 2.850 metres where -- and I try to compare these figures with the scenarios that you had to analyse and I see that scenario number 3 actually is 2.825 metres. Can you explain this difference?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The distance is 2.825 metres. That's the real situation in scenario number 3 and the distance between the points is 2.825 metres. When I carried out my test, I selected the altitude of 2.800 -- the distance of 2.850 metres, and I had an item on the ground, and I wanted to be certain that that was the position in question. But 25 metres doesn't mean much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned that you used binoculars to perform this test around Sarajevo. Do you recall what type of binoculars you were using and what this allows you to perform?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: I used a 10X50 binoculars. These binoculars has a marking which says 125 through 1.000 on the binoculars. That means when you use the binoculars at something at a distance of a thousand metres, it's as if you're looking at an object with the naked eye at a distance of 125 metres. So I would say that this pair of binoculars belongs to the category of fairly good and high performance binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you know thousand these binoculars compare with the binoculars used by the warring factions during the war in 1993 in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Well, on the whole in Bosnia in the course of the war, military binoculars is 6 X 30 or 7 X 40 were used, and these binoculars are not as good as the ones I used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I refer you to tab 22, and would I like you to explain what this is.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: These are technical instructions for hand-held binoculars, 6 X 30, from the year 1969, and it contains all the technical information necessary for these binoculars. And these binoculars, 6 X 30, have the possibility of magnifying an image six times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I refer you to page 79 in the attachment in your language, which corresponds to in the English translation to page 5, and ask you whether this is the information that says a 6 X 30 binoculars will increase by six times.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you now turn --

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: You can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- to tab number 23 and tell us what this is. I -- just for the record, I would like to state that tab number 22 was Defence Exhibit 1640.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: These are the technical instructions for the RD 7 X 40 C binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at page 2 of this instruction, and most particularly 1.2, what information do we find there?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Well, you have the technical details here, and first thing mentioned is that these binoculars magnify the image seven times. The binoculars that I use magnified the image observed eight times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now proceed to tab number 24 and look at the chart you referred to a little earlier, and I would like to know first what is meant by the plus and the minus signs in the chart. As I said, in the upper horizontal table you have the distance I was interested in, 850 metres, 1.400 metres, 2.550 metres, 2.700 metres, 2.825 metres, and 3.050 metres. These are the distances used in the scenarios for directions for which we established that there was optical visibility. And from these distances -- for these distances I provided answers to these questions by using a test, by making a test, by observing with the naked eye and with a pair of binoculars. If we have a plus in the column this means that visibility was possible and the answer to the question put was affirmative. If we have a minus then the answer to the question put is negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would ask you whether you can inform the Trial Chamber whether the results of your practical tests compared -- how did they compare with the theory found in the books that we saw earlier and whether these conclusions are a mix of both or just a practical test.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: These results fully fit in with the theory that I was able to study.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now refer you to tab number 25 and ask you whether the information included in this table correspond to your conclusions on the 15 scenarios that were put to you.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think this is a good time for a break, and after the break I'll need another 15 minutes to show a few photographs that might help the witness facilitate the Chamber's work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's half past twelve. We'll have a 20- to 25-minute break, and we will resume at about five to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, please resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Izmirlic, just before the break, you confirmed that tab 25 contained your conclusions. I would like you to turn to tab 25, and I just have a few questions to ask you in respect of the table that we found there. My first question relates to scenario number 2, and in scenario number 2 there is a mention with respect to the possibility to see -- possibility to see persons setting houses on fire, and what your conclusion is that this is not possible with the naked eye, and then in the box beside, with binoculars you say, "to distinguish yes movement only but to see, no." Can you further explain what you mean by this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: At a distance of 850 metres, it is possible to see people, people in movement. But as to the uniforms they're wearing, the suit, the clothes they're wearing, the objects that they have in their hands, whether it's a rifle or a stick or a canister of some kind that is being carried in order to set houses on fire, these are things that are impossible to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question relates to scenario number 3 from Strmac to Brajkovici. And again the conclusion was with respect to persons. Now, we see the distance here is 2.825 metres, and with respect to persons you say that you cannot see a person with the naked eye, but you can see a person with binoculars, and again you have to distinguish and to see. Can you provide further information?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Well, I provide the same answer that I gave you to your previous question. You can see people at that distance if you use a pair of binoculars. It's possible to see a man from that distance. You can see the outline of a man. You can see that there is someone moving, and you can distinguish a man from a tree observed from the same distance, or from an electricity pole. But as to the uniform or the clothes worn by that person, as to what that person has in his hands, as to the weapon carried by that person, these are things that one cannot see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question relates to scenario number 4 from Strmac to Grahovcici in Milika, at a distance of 1.400 metres. Your conclusion with respect to persons looting and persons setting houses on fire. According to what this chart says, your answer is no for all of them, but I say to distinguish movement, yes, with binoculars. What do you mean by this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: At a distance of 1.400 metres, if you're using binoculars, a pair of binoculars, a fairly powerful pair of binoculars, for example the pair of binoculars that magnifies seven times, then it's as if you were observing something with the naked eye from a distance of 250 metres, and this means that it's possible to see the movements that people make. It's possible to distinguish a person, but you can't see what the person is doing. You can't see whether such a person is setting fire to a house. You can see fire and smoke from such a distance, but you can't see the precise act that such an individual would be involved in. You can't see whether he has a rifle on him or something else, a video, for example. That's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, for all of these scenarios, and I'm talking about from 2 to 7, did you bear in mind the other factors that you mentioned at the beginning of your testimony? Namely, you said the day, the season, the weather. Did you take those into consideration, or are those included in your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. This is a very important factor. How the feature faces the observer and the position of the sun, these are very important factors, and I assumed that these factors were very favourable, that the conditions were ideal for an observer. That was my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was there a reason for doing so?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: I wanted to be both objective and very strict with myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I have one last question with respect to the use of binoculars. Is there a -- something particular about the use of binoculars when it comes to seeing objects in the distance?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: First of all, visibility must be good. If you turn a pair of binoculars to the sun, the effect is very poor. And as I have already said, if you have a 10 X 50 binoculars, you have the marking 125/1000 on the binoculars. But according to that logic, if you have the distance of 2.000 that would be 250 through 2.000, not because of the way in which the binoculars were constructed, but the mathematics I mentioned can be applied for distances up to 2.000 metres. If you have greater distances, these accusations are -- can no longer be applied, because if you use binoculars for distances over 2.000 metres, the image you obtain is fuzzy. You have a very unclear image.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, Mr. Izmirlic, is whether there are other ways to make the same determinations as you have made in your conclusions, for example, using a camera, or is there another way to do this?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but if you use a camera, I would say that the technical equipment has made a lot of progress in this field. I couldn't prove this scientifically, though, but my colleague who was supposed to -- to come Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and testify here made an experiment with a camera, but because there was a lot of snow in Sarajevo, he made this experiment in similar terrain in the area of Mostar. He photographed certain features, certain people from certain distances. However, I can confirm that I couldn't claim scientifically that this is a hundred per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I ask you to turn to tab number 26 and explain to us if you know what this is.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from a topographic map, the scale of which was -- or is 1:50000, sector Mostar 2. And my colleague was down there, as I have said. I wasn't there, but I'm fully familiar with the method that was used. The segment I'm now indicating is in the Mostar area at the place of Podgorani. In that area, detail certain features were selected, houses, auxiliary facilities, lorries, a jeep, a group of people, some of whom were in military uniform, whereas others were wearing civilian clothes. And a camera was used, a Olympus camera, recently manufactured was used, and this camera has a zoom that can magnify the image five times. These objects were photographed from a distance of 100, 200, 500, 1.000, 1.500 metres, 2.000 metres, 3.000 metres, 5.000 metres, and up to 7.000 metres. They went up to that distance from the objects I have already mentioned. These objects were photographed twice. The first time they were photographed in an ordinary manner, and the second time they were photographed with this zoom that magnifies the image five times. And according to the theory, if you have a zoom that magnifies an image five times, you obtain an image which resembles the image you would have if you observed those features with the naked eye from those distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you turn quickly to tab number 27 and tell the Trial Chamber whether this is the type of camera which was used to perform this test by your colleague.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the camera used. You've got a photograph of the camera, and you have technical instructions and technical details on the camera. I've seen this camera and I was also shown photographs that were provided on a CD. So if possible, I would be grateful if we could have a look at those photographs too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's do that, Mr. Izmirlic. I will start with the first photograph, and you can explain to the Trial Chamber what this picture actually is. You can look at your screen, and you will actually see the photo number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll take advantage of this opportunity to confirm that all the photographs, as well as all the graphical analysis, are part of just one number or one Defence document that has been provided to the Prosecution. I believe that the number was 1978, but I'll have to confirm this because I haven't got the exact number on me. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... comment on this first picture.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, this is the area around Mostar. The settlement is called Podgorani. A detail was selected on a relatively flat ground, and two houses. One is a garage and some out-houses, a truck, a military jeep, and a passenger car. Several people in a group, two of whom are in uniform. Then there are also some children. And this segment appears on the photographs, and this photograph was taken at a distance of 100 metres. Now we will see the same image zoomed in five times. If everything is all right with the equipment, this would be what the naked eye can see. Next photograph at a distance of 200 metres. So we can run through the rest of the photographs quickly. A normal photograph without a zoom at a distance of 200 metres. The segments as listed a moment ago appear on the photograph in this way. Zoomed in five times, this is what one gets. We can move on. The same picture taken from a distance of 500 metres without you zooming in. Now, with the zoom, this is the result. I think it is already quite clear that on this photograph already it is hard to distinguish the uniforms. The truck is visible, and if one makes an effort, you can see the small car. The buildings are still visible. Next one, please. A photograph taken at a distance of 1.000 metres without zoom. Now, next one with the zoom. Here is the photograph at a distance of 1.000 metres, and the visible ability of the observer at certain distances. In this case, we can see the truck. And you can distinguish between the big and the small car, and this was confirmed by my tests. However, you can see that the people can only just be discerned. Next, please. Can we have 1.500 metres, please, or 2.000? This is a photograph taken from a distance of 2.000 metres without the zoom. Now, with the zoom. This is again a photograph without the zoom taken at a distance of 3.000 metres. Now, with the zoom, please. This is when we zoom in, and it is still possible to distinguish the houses. It is possible to identify the houses, the tables, and other out-houses. A photograph from a distance of 5.000 metres without the zoom. Now, with the zoom, please. It is still possible to identify the buildings at a distance of 5.000 metres, and this is confirmed by theory which says that at that distance it is still possible to distinguish the buildings. One more, please. Yes. With an ordinary zoom you see a kind of haze. This is at 7.000 metres. It is not a subject of discussion, but we see from this what it is possible to see from a distance of 7.000 metres, just a haze. As I was saying, we wanted to show in this way, too, what one can see, but I cannot assert this 100 per cent because the technology is making great advances and anything is possible nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Izmirlic, I just have one last question for you, and this is simply to ask you whether on the basis of all the tests that you performed, both the topographic test on the map as well as using those rules found in military manuals and the own tests that you have performed in the area of Sarajevo, I am not talking about the pictures, to what degree can you confirm that your conclusions in the chart found in tab 24 are accurate? Tab 25, sorry. Tab 25 is the 15 scenarios.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: On the basis of my training, on the basis of my personal experience, on the basis of my research, I claim with certainty and full responsibility that these indications are correct, that is that my conclusions are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one last question, Mr. Izmirlic, with respect to the pictures. You concluded that this was not scientific information, but do those pictures provide a good idea as to what can be seen from various distances with the naked eye?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: I believe they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Izmirlic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has completed its examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Izmirlic.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My name is Daryl Mundis, and along with my colleagues here today we represent the Prosecution in this case. I have a number of questions that I'll be asking you. It's clear, given the time, that we won't finish today, sir, but I'll at least get started. Before I do that, though, let me assure you that my intention is not in any way to confuse you, so I would ask if you don't understand my question to simply say so and I'll rephrase the question so that you do understand what it is that I'm asking you. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start out, sir, with a little bit of basics. Can you just tell us a little bit about what the speciality of military topography is all about?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Military topography. It doesn't have to be military topography. "Topos" means a place. "Grapho" means to write. In other words, a description of a place or the land.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what specific features of the science of topography relate to the military?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: The main tactical topographical categories of the land which have some bearing on defensive activity, and those are, under number 1, the relief of the land, hydrography, vegetation, communications, roads, settlements, population, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me ask you some questions about what it was precisely that you were asked to do by the Defence in this case. Could you tell us, please, what instructions you received from the Defence counsel in this case with respect to the tasks that you were asked to do?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: I was asked to make an assessment of observations in these locations, and the scenarios 1 to 17 -- or, rather, the seventh, fourteenth, and sixteenth are identical. The points of observation and the objects of observation are the same, so we concluded there was a total of 15 different directions. From the Defence, itches simply asked to select the most favourable positions for points A and B, if we can call them that. Point A is always the place or the position from which somebody was doing the observing. So my task was to make an assessment of the visibility from those points to those B points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you were given this task, can you tell us a little bit about how you went about performing that task? How did you start? What did you do? What methods did you use, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: First of all, I had to select a set of maps of that area to be able to identify those points. It is simplest to work with the mentioned set of maps, that is set 5, in the scale 1:25000, because they are the largest, the most accurate, and the most detailed. And as someone who used to work on designing those same maps, I can claim that their reliability is 100 per cent. So I first had to identify those points. After that, I had to mark those points with the letters A and B, as I did, to link those points with a straight line and to analyse the position of the ground or the configuration of the land in between. As a topographer can at each point on the map determine the altitude, what is shown on that map. Is it a house, a stream, flowing water, or a river that is flowing? A river that is flowing constantly or one that can occasionally dry up. Then on that same map, there is the vegetation, which is mostly marked in green, whereas the altitudes in this case were indicated with isohypses. And I said a moment ago that those were closed curves linking points of the same altitude. Then also there are trigonometric points and grid points. And on these maps there are main and auxiliary points at an equidistance of 10 metres. The equidistance is the vertical distance between two neighbouring isohypses. So it is possible to say with certainty within a metre the altitude of any point on the map, and this was important for assessing visibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me ask you this question about the maps and this procedure or process that you undertook. Did you use paper maps or did you use computer generated maps or the paper maps having been scanned into the computer in order to conduct the analysis and create the maps that we have with us here in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: No. I had the original printed topographic maps such as they exist in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the federal defence ministry, we have all sections of topographic maps covering the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the scale 1:25000, 50.000, 200.000 and a review topographic map of 1:500000. And I am in a possibility to pick up this map, not just me, any official or soldier, to -- we are able to use those maps, so that I used those maps printed from a matrix.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly then, sir, you simply took a paper version of the 1:25000 map and made the calculations that we have before us in the binder today.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the information that you relied on in doing your computations is all reflected on the map.

utterances.speaker: ABID IZMIRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The map has all the scales. I did take with me the originals of those maps, at least most of the originals of those maps. So I have them in the scale of 1:250000. And each map contains information, the most important being the scale of the map, which means that if it says 1:25000, that is sufficient indication for me that 1 millimetre on the map relates to 25 metres in nature, or 1 centimetre equals 250 metres. And that applies to the entire area covered by that map. Which means that if we measure the distance between Sarajevo and Zenica on a map in millimetres and multiply the millimetres with the scale, we will find that it is 72 kilometres. Another indicator that is probably of interest to you is how I compute the heights.
